steps.title: Video: Hand Hygiene for Caregivers
steps.caption: CDC guidance on proper hand-washing and sanitizer use to prevent infections.

steps.title: Interactive: Hand-Washing Steps
steps.content:
WHEN TO WASH HANDS
- Before putting on gloves and after removing them.
- Before and after touching a client.
- After toileting or changing incontinence products.
- After touching contaminated surfaces, laundry, or trash.
- Before food preparation and eating.

SOAP AND WATER STEPS (20 SECONDS)
1. Wet hands with clean, running water.
2. Apply soap and lather the backs of hands, between fingers, and under nails.
3. Scrub for at least 20 seconds (sing Happy Birthday twice).
4. Rinse under clean, running water.
5. Dry with a clean towel or air dryer.
6. Use the towel to turn off the faucet if possible.

ALCOHOL-BASED HAND RUB
- Use when hands are not visibly soiled.
- Apply enough product to cover all hand surfaces.
- Rub until dry, about 20 seconds.

steps.title: Interactive: PPE & Exposure Response
steps.content:
PUTTING ON PPE (DONNING)
1. Perform hand hygiene.
2. Put on gown, if needed, opening at the back and tying securely.
3. Put on mask or respirator; mold the nose piece and secure straps.
4. Put on eye protection if splashes are possible.
5. Put on gloves last, extending over gown cuffs.

TAKING OFF PPE (DOFFING)
1. Remove gloves first, turning them inside out.
2. Remove gown by untying and rolling away from you.
3. Remove eye protection and mask.
4. Perform hand hygiene immediately.

EXPOSURE RESPONSE
- Needlestick or blood exposure: wash or flush the area immediately and report to the office.
- Seek medical evaluation promptly.
- Hepatitis B vaccine is offered to staff at risk of blood exposure.
- TB screening is required upon hire and reviewed annually.

LAUNDRY & KITCHEN
- Handle soiled laundry carefully; do not shake.
- Bag waste securely and follow local biohazard rules.
- Keep food prep areas clean and separate raw and cooked foods.

steps.title: TB & Bloodborne Pathogens
steps.content:
BLOODBORNE PATHOGENS
Bloodborne pathogens are infectious microorganisms in human blood that can cause disease. The most common are Hepatitis B Virus (HBV), Hepatitis C Virus (HCV), and HIV.

MODES OF TRANSMISSION
- Direct contact of blood or body fluids with broken skin or mucous membranes.
- Indirect contact through contaminated surfaces or objects.
- Needlestick or sharp injuries.
They are NOT spread by casual contact, hugging, coughing, or sharing toilets.

PREVENTION
- Treat all blood and body fluids as potentially infectious.
- Use gloves and appropriate PPE.
- Never recap needles; dispose of sharps in approved containers.
- Clean and disinfect contaminated surfaces immediately.

TUBERCULOSIS
TB is a bacterial infection that usually affects the lungs. It spreads through the air when an infected person coughs or sneezes. Screening is required upon hire and reviewed annually.

IF EXPOSED
Wash the area with soap and water, flush splashes, notify your supervisor, complete an incident report, and seek medical evaluation promptly.

steps.title: Respiratory Illness & Exposure Control
steps.content:
RESPIRATORY HYGIENE
Coughs and sneezes spread germs. Cover your mouth and nose with a tissue or elbow, dispose of tissues promptly, and perform hand hygiene.

WHEN A CLIENT HAS FLU OR COVID SYMPTOMS
- Put on a mask and gloves before close contact.
- Encourage rest and fluids.
- Monitor temperature and symptoms.
- Call the office and the client's physician for guidance.
- Wash hands often and clean high-touch surfaces.

WHEN TO SEEK URGENT CARE
- Difficulty breathing or chest pain.
- Confusion or sudden dizziness.
- Persistent high fever.
- Signs of dehydration such as very dark urine, dry mouth, or no urination for 8 or more hours.

PROTECTING YOURSELF
Stay home if you are sick and report it to the office. Get an annual flu vaccine when available and keep your immunizations up to date.
